t: Minimum Swaps to Move Zeros to End
o: We must rearrange the array so every 0 sits after every non-zero element, using as few swaps as possible. Each swap exchanges any two elements, so we want the minimum number of transpositions needed. In Example 1, [0,1,0,3,12] needs 2 swaps: one zero is swapped with 3 and the other with 12. In Example 2, a single swap of nums[0]=0 with nums[3]=2 fixes everything. Example 3 already has all zeros at the end, so the answer is 0. With n up to 100, even an O(n^2) simulation passes easily, but an O(n) two-pointer solution exists.
k: The answer equals the number of (zero, non-zero) pairs where the zero appears before the non-zero element.
A single left-to-right pass counting zeros seen so far gives this number: whenever a non-zero is found, it must cross every zero encountered earlier.
Each counted pair corresponds to exactly one necessary swap, so the count is both achievable and optimal.

a.i: Repeatedly scan for a 0 followed later by a non-zero and swap them directly, like pushing bubbles. Each such swap fixes at least one misplaced zero against one non-zero, and we keep going until no such pair remains. This mirrors how many people first think about the problem and is easy to reason about, though slower.
s: Initialize swaps = 0 and repeat until no change occurs in a full pass.
In each pass, for every index i with nums[i] == 0, find the nearest j > i with nums[j] != 0.
If found, swap nums[i] and nums[j] and increment swaps.
Stop when a complete pass performs no swaps.
a.t: O(n^2) per pass in the worst case, with up to O(n) passes, giving O(n^3) worst case — fine for n <= 100 but not scalable.
a.sp: O(1) extra space — only counters and in-place swaps.

a.i: Every non-zero element that has some zero before it must end up after those zeros, requiring one swap per crossing pair. So the minimum number of swaps equals the total number of (zero-before, non-zero-after) inversions. We can compute this in one pass: keep a running count of zeros; each time we meet a non-zero element, add the current zero count to the answer. This greedy pairing is optimal because each swap can resolve at most one such pair.
s: Iterate through the array left to right.
Otherwise add zeros to ans (this non-zero must cross all zeros seen so far).
a.t: O(n) — a single pass over the array with constant work per element.

w: Prefer Approach 2 in an interview: it is a single linear pass, trivially correct, and generalizes (e.g., 'move zeros to front' or 'minimum adjacent swaps' variants). A common pitfall is confusing this with the classic 'move zeroes' problem where you only need to overwrite in place — here you must count swaps. Another pitfall is assuming relative order of non-zeros matters; it does not, which is why counting inversion pairs suffices. Edge cases: array with no zeros (answer 0), all zeros (answer 0), and a single element. Follow-ups might ask for the actual sequence of swaps (use two pointers swapping each zero forward) or the version restricted to adjacent swaps (same formula, since adjacent swaps also cost one per inversion).
